Md Fazlul Karim with Khandker Aminul Haque, Advocates ----- For the Petitioner. 
Md Israfil Hossain, Advocate ----- For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Aumullaya Chandra Halder ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Md Mohsin Ali Mandal and ors. ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule, was obtained by the preemptor-petitioner of the Miscellaneous Case No. 36/1994 upon making an application for revision under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure against judgment and order dated 13-7-1998 passed by the learned District Judges, Serajganj in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 37 of 1997 upholding those of the Senior Assistant Judge, Ullapara, Serajganj, in the above stated preemption case passed on 10-7-1997. 

 2. Essential facts for disposal of this Rule are that the petitioner or Aumullaya Chandra Halder filed the aforesaid case on 31-10-1994 to have the case land measuring 21 decimals preempted which was transferred by his brother PW 2 Sarat Chandra Halder to the stranger opposite party No. 1 Mohsin Ali MandaI on 13-9-1994 by a registered kabala. The petitioner is a co-sharer in the case holding and he deposited the consideration amount of the kabala under preemption amounting to Taka 7,000 along with statutory compensation as required under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 3. The opposite party No. 1 Mohsin Ali Mandal contested the case stating, inter alia, that the deposit of money was insufficient as the consideration of the sale was fixed at Taka 40,000 which was actually paid by the transferee and also stated in the bainapatra executed prior to the execution of the sale deed. It is contended further that the petitioner being full brother of the vendor was aware of the sale transaction from the very beginning and knew about the agreement for sale. At that time, the petitioner not only consented to the sale transaction but also refused to purchase the case land. Due to such knowledge and consent of the co-sharer petitioner the sale deed was executed and registered showing lesser amount of consideration than actually paid. 

 4. The learned Assistant Judge recorded evidence of 3 witnesses for the petitioner and 6 witnesses of the opposite party No. 1 and after hearing; he dismissed the miscellaneous case with the findings that the case land under presumption being homestead land preemption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is not maintainable. That the petitioner knowing fully well about the actual sale values of Taka 49,000 deposited only Taka 7,000 with compensation thereof which was inadequate and that he did not exercise option to purchase the case land at that time. 

 7. Mr Md Fazlul Karim, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submits that the courts below have overlooked the specific provision of section 96(3)(a) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act wherein the consideration of the kabala under preemption together with compensation thereof is necessary to be deposited at the time of submitting application for preemption, Since the petitioner has complied with this legal requirement, the question of inadequate deposit does not arise. 

 9. On perusal of the certified copy of the oral evidence adduced before the learned trial Court (supplied by the learned Advocate for that petitioner at the time of hearing) it appears that there was an agreement in between the parties for the execution and registration of a sale deed the said bainapatra dated 14-2-1994 has been produced and admitted in evidence. It transpires that the consideration money settled in between the parties is stated to be Taka 40,000 in the bainapatra and earnest money of Taka 18,000 was paid on the date of agreement. In this respect, several witnesses including the scribe of thesale deed and bainapatra (OP W-6) and attesting witness of bainapatra (OPW 2) gave uncontroverted testimony about payment of Taka 40,000 as consideration of the transaction Both the courts below have found concurrently that the case land was sold at Taka 40,000 out of which Taka 18,000 was paid in advance on the date of execution of bainapatra. I do not find any reason to disagree with such finding arrived at on the basis of credible evidence on record. But the fact remains that the transferee is not entitled to claim consideration money in excess of the amount mentioned in the deed of transfer itself as contemplated under proviso to the sub-section 3(b) of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Besides the basic requirements of making deposit is provided in sub- section 3(a) of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which runs as follows: 

 "An application made under sub-section I shall be dismissed unless the applicant or applicants at the time of making it deposited in the court the amount of consideration money or the value of the transferred holding or portion or share of the holding as stated in the notice under section 89 or in the deed of transfer as the case may be together with compensation of the rate of ten percentage of such amount." 

 12. For the reasons stated above, I do not find any legal infirmity in the impugned judgment and order passed by the learned appellate Court and, as such, it should be maintained.
